## Key Messages {.unnumbered}

- LLM-driven multi-agent systems may be the most important way to **scale test-time compute beyond one agent**: beyond one context window, one memory state, and one serial reasoning path.
- A single agent can think longer, but only up to a point. Multi-agent systems can think wider: many attempts, tools, memories, critiques, experiments, and artifact branches.
- They are best understood as **coordinated test-time work over separately stateful attempts** rather than as role play among chatbots.
- Classical MAS and MARL remain useful warnings, but modern LLM multi-agent systems emerged from a different substrate: agent harnesses, tools, memory, artifacts, benchmarks, and test-time orchestration.
- The 2023 wave made multi-agent LLM systems visible through simulated organizations, debate, social simulation, software teams, and conversation-programming frameworks.
- The 2024-2026 evidence is more discriminating: many apparent gains weaken under realistic benchmarks, equal inference budgets, stronger single-agent baselines, cost accounting, repeated trials, and long-horizon artifact evaluation.
- Multiple agents help through identifiable mechanisms: independent attempts, heterogeneous evidence, critique, specialization, branch-and-merge artifact work, shared memory, human-governed portfolios, and optimized or trained coordination.
- Multiple agents hurt when the task fits in one context, messages are lossy, agents share the same blind spots, validators are weak, shared state is contaminated, or coordination cost exceeds the value of extra attempts.
- Coordination need not be hand-written forever. A growing line of work optimizes topology, routing, workflow structure, MAS generation, and agent-level collaboration behavior, but current evidence is still narrow and must be tested under transfer, cost, safety, and long-horizon artifact constraints.
- The central unit of analysis is not agent count. It is useful work per unit of cost, latency, risk, and human review bandwidth.
